prompt: Using the commuting table, how many more Grade $9$ students than Grade $10$ students do NOT take the bus?
hint: Students who do not take the bus either walk or go by car. Find that count for each grade before comparing.

hints.text: Students who do not take the bus either walk or go by car. Find that count for each grade before comparing.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try it small: if a column totals $20$ and $8$ of them ride the bus, then $12$ do not. Subtracting from the column total is faster than adding the other rows.
Subtract the bus riders from each column total. Grade $9$ has $110 - 45$ and Grade $10$ has $90 - 35$. Then subtract the two results.
The counts are $65$ and $55$, so there are $65 - 55 = 10$ more Grade $9$ students who do not take the bus.

learningObjective: Combine complement and comparison steps on a two-way table.
explanation: In Grade $9$, the students not taking the bus number $110 - 45 = 65$, which matches $30 + 35$ from the other rows.
In Grade $10$, the students not taking the bus number $90 - 35 = 55$, which matches $20 + 35$.
Subtract to compare the grades: $65 - 55 = 10$, so there are $10$ more such students in Grade $9$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Subtracting from the total beats adding rows
steps: Adding $30 + 35$ works, but with four or five commute categories the complement is much faster.
Column total minus the excluded row gives the "not" count in one step.
The complement also generalizes: for probability, $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$ is the same idea.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Adding rows you did not need, or answering 65 (one grade's count) instead of the difference, are the designed exits.
Complement per column first — 110 − 45 and 90 − 35 — then subtract. Two clean complements beat three additions.
